items.name: Metformin
hx: ↑ hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↓ insulin sensitivity (AMPK)
Both arrows are reversed: it cuts liver glucose output and improves sensitivity.
↓ intestinal carbohydrate digestion (α-glucosidase block)
That's acarbose; metformin cuts hepatic glucose output.
Replaces insulin action at GLUT2 in the liver
It isn't an insulin substitute; it reduces liver glucose output and improves sensitivity.
items.sewhy: Metformin concentrates in gut cells, causing GI upset; it reduces B12 absorption, and because it inhibits mitochondrial lactate use, it can accumulate in renal failure and cause lactic acidosis.

x: Builds up and stimulates insulin release → hypoglycaemia
Metformin doesn't release insulin and alone rarely causes hypos; accumulation risks lactic acidosis.
Nephrotoxic → speeds CKD progression
Not nephrotoxic; it accumulates and risks lactic acidosis.
Hepatically cleared, so no change is needed
It's renally cleared; stop it below eGFR 30.

ci.why: Hypoxic tissues make lactate the kidneys can't clear: pause (sick day rules)
x: Illness raises glucose so much that metformin fails: double the dose
Pause it: hypoxia and AKI raise the risk of lactic acidosis.
Vomiting stops absorption: switch to IV metformin
There's no IV metformin; pause it during acute illness.
Infection makes metformin cause hypos: pause until eating
The danger is lactic acidosis, not hypos.
Contrast binds metformin and inactivates it
No binding; contrast-induced AKI can make metformin accumulate.
Metformin makes contrast directly nephrotoxic
The risk is AKI trapping metformin (lactic acidosis).
Contrast triggers hypoglycaemia with metformin
Not hypos; lactic acidosis if AKI develops.
The liver normally activates metformin
Metformin isn't a prodrug; the liver clears lactate.
Metformin is hepatotoxic in cirrhosis
Not hepatotoxic; impaired lactate clearance risks acidosis.
Alcohol speeds metformin excretion
No; poor liver lactate clearance is the issue.
Adds to the ketone load
It doesn't make ketones; it adds lactic acidosis risk.
Causes hyperkalaemia
Not the reason; it adds to acidosis.
Blocks insulin absorption
No; it adds to metabolic acidosis.

items.name: Sulfonylureas
items.how: Close β-cell K_ATP channels → insulin release regardless of glucose
hx: Open β-cell K_ATP channels → insulin release only when glucose is high
They close K_ATP channels, releasing insulin whatever the glucose (hence hypos).
Close β-cell K_ATP channels → insulin release only when glucose is high
Release happens regardless of glucose, which is why hypos occur.
Block glucagon release from α-cells → lower glucose
They act on β-cells to release insulin.
items.sewhy: They make beta cells release insulin whatever the glucose level, causing hypoglycaemia and weight gain (insulin is anabolic).

x: Needs working α-cells
They act on β-cells, which type 1 lacks.
Needs normal kidneys
Not the reason; type 1 has no β-cells to stimulate.
Needs insulin resistance
No; it needs functioning β-cells.
Shortened action → hyperglycaemia
They accumulate, causing prolonged hypos.
Direct nephrotoxicity → AKI
Not nephrotoxic; accumulation causes severe hypos.
Prolonged action → weight loss
They cause weight gain; accumulation causes hypos.
Neonatal hyperglycaemia; use metformin
They cross the placenta and cause neonatal hypos; insulin is used.
Fetal macrosomia; use a DPP-4 inhibitor
The concern is neonatal hypoglycaemia; insulin is the safe choice.
Fetal kidney damage; use an SGLT2 inhibitor
No; neonatal hypoglycaemia, so use insulin.
Weight loss risk
They cause weight gain; hypos are the concern.
Ketoacidosis risk
The concern is hypoglycaemia.
Dehydration risk
Not dehydration; hypos.

items.name: SGLT2 inhibitors
items.how: Block glucose (and Na⁺) reabsorption in the proximal tubule → glycosuria
hx: Block glucose (and Na⁺) reabsorption in the collecting duct → glycosuria
SGLT2 sits in the proximal tubule.
Block glucose absorption in the small intestine → osmotic diarrhoea
They act in the kidney, not the gut.
Stimulate glucose secretion into the loop of Henle → glycosuria
They stop glucose being reabsorbed; they don't secrete it.
items.sewhy: Glucose in the urine feeds genital and urinary infections; the osmotic diuresis causes volume depletion; lower insulin needs favour ketone production (DKA with near-normal glucose).

ci.why: Risk of DKA with near-normal glucose
x: Risk of severe hypoglycaemia
Alone they rarely cause hypos; the danger is DKA with near-normal glucose.
Risk of a hyperosmolar state with very high glucose
The DKA they cause can have near-normal glucose.
Risk of worsening insulin resistance
No; the risk is DKA with near-normal glucose.

ci.c: Acute illness or dehydration (sick day rules)
ci.why: Osmotic diuresis worsens dehydration; ketosis risk
x: Glucose retention worsens hyperglycaemia; hypo risk
They cause glucose and water loss (osmotic diuresis) and ketosis.
Sodium retention worsens oedema; heart failure risk
They lose sodium and water; dehydration and ketosis are the risks.
Osmotic diuresis worsens dehydration; hypoglycaemia risk
The other risk is ketosis (DKA), not hypos.
Proven teratogen
No proven harm; there's no safety data, so insulin is used.
Causes fetal glycosuria
Not the stated reason; there's no safety data.
Causes preterm labour
No; there's simply no safety data.

items.name: GLP-1 receptor agonists
items.how: Glucose-dependent insulin release, ↓ glucagon, slower gastric emptying, ↓ appetite
hx: Stimulate insulin receptors directly, ↑ glucose uptake into muscle
They act on GLP-1 receptors, boosting insulin only when glucose is high.
Glucose-dependent insulin release, ↓ glucagon, faster gastric emptying, ↑ appetite
They slow gastric emptying and reduce appetite (hence weight loss).
Block liver glucagon receptors, ↓ glucose output only
They lower glucagon release, but also boost insulin, slow emptying and reduce appetite.
items.sewhy: Slowing gastric emptying and acting on brain satiety centres cause nausea and vomiting; rapid weight loss promotes gallstones, and pancreatitis has been reported.

ci.why: Can trigger acute pancreatitis; stop if suspected
x: Can cause chronic pancreatic insufficiency; add enzymes
The risk is acute pancreatitis; stop if suspected.
Can cause pancreatic cancer; screen yearly
No proven link; the caution is acute pancreatitis.
Can cause hypoglycaemia; halve the dose
Not the reason; acute pancreatitis risk.

ci.c: Personal/family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2
ci.why: C-cell tumours in animal studies (a formal contraindication in US labelling)
x: Follicular cell tumours in human trials (a formal contraindication in UK labelling)
The signal was C-cell tumours in rodents; it's a formal contraindication only in the US.
Iodine content worsens thyroid cancer (a contraindication worldwide)
No iodine; the concern is rodent C-cell tumours.
TSH suppression speeds tumour growth (a contraindication in all labelling)
Not through TSH; C-cell tumours were seen in animals.
Double the dose in pregnancy
They're stopped before conception.
Switch to a sulfonylurea
Stop before conception; insulin is used if needed.
Continue: proven safe
Not proven safe; stop before conception.

ci.why: Rapid glucose fall can worsen retinopathy
x: Raised BP can worsen retinopathy
They lower BP if anything; a rapid glucose fall is the concern.
A slow glucose fall can worsen retinopathy
It's a rapid fall (early worsening) that's the problem.
Drug deposits build up in the retina
No; rapid glucose lowering can worsen retinopathy.

items.name: DPP-4 inhibitors
items.how: Block breakdown of endogenous GLP-1 and GIP
hx: Speed breakdown of endogenous glucagon
They block DPP-4, which breaks down GLP-1 and GIP.
Block breakdown of endogenous insulin in the liver
They protect incretins (GLP-1, GIP), not insulin.
Block GLP-1 and GIP receptors
They raise incretin levels; blocking receptors would do the opposite.
items.sewhy: They raise endogenous incretins modestly, so side effects are few; pancreatitis is rare.

x: Associated with gallstone ileus
The association is with acute pancreatitis.
Associated with pancreatic insufficiency
No; acute pancreatitis.
Associated with hypercalcaemia
Not the reason; acute pancreatitis.
Cause DKA in type 1
They don't cause DKA; they're just not enough without insulin.
Destroy any remaining β-cells
No; they're insufficient on their own.
Cause severe hypos in type 1
Alone they rarely cause hypos; they're insufficient.

items.name: Pioglitazone
hx: PPAR-α agonist → ↓ triglycerides
That's fibrates; pioglitazone activates PPAR-γ.
PPAR-γ antagonist → ↑ insulin secretion
It activates PPAR-γ, improving insulin sensitivity.
Insulin receptor agonist → ↑ glucose uptake
It works through PPAR-γ gene effects.
items.sewhy: PPAR-γ activation makes the kidney retain sodium and water (oedema, heart failure), promotes fat storage (weight gain) and shifts bone precursors away from bone (fractures).

x: Negative inotropy precipitates failure
It causes fluid retention, not weaker contraction.
Hypokalaemia precipitates arrhythmias
No; fluid retention precipitates failure.
Raised afterload precipitates failure
The issue is fluid retention.
Linked to kidney stones
The link is with bladder cancer.
Linked to renal cell cancer
No; bladder cancer.
Linked to UTIs
That's SGLT2 inhibitors; pioglitazone is linked to bladder cancer.
Nephrotoxic
The concern is liver toxicity.
Causes hypoglycaemia
Not the reason; it's hepatotoxic.
Raises ammonia
No; it's hepatotoxic.

items.name: Insulin
items.how: Replaces insulin: glucose uptake (GLUT4), ↓ gluconeogenesis, drives K⁺ into cells
hx: Replaces insulin: glucose uptake (GLUT2), ↑ gluconeogenesis, drives K⁺ out of cells
Insulin drives glucose in through GLUT4, suppresses gluconeogenesis and moves K⁺ into cells.
Stimulates the pancreas: more insulin release, ↓ glucagon, drives K⁺ into cells
It's given as insulin itself; it doesn't stimulate the pancreas.
Blocks glucagon: ↓ glycogenolysis only, drives K⁺ out of cells
It acts on insulin receptors and moves K⁺ into cells.
items.sewhy: Too much insulin relative to food causes hypoglycaemia; it's anabolic (weight gain), injecting in the same spot causes fatty lumps, and it drives potassium into cells.

x: Will raise glucose too fast
It lowers glucose further.
Won't work until glucose is normal
It still works, lowering glucose further.
Causes hyperkalaemia
It lowers K⁺; the issue is glucose falling further.

ci.why: Pushes K⁺ into cells → arrhythmias; replace K⁺ in DKA
x: Pulls K⁺ out of cells → hyperkalaemia; withhold K⁺ in DKA
Insulin pushes K⁺ into cells; replace K⁺ as you treat DKA.
Increases urinary K⁺ loss → cramps; give spironolactone
The fall is a shift into cells; replace K⁺.
Pushes K⁺ into cells → seizures; give calcium in DKA
The danger is arrhythmias; replace K⁺.

ci.why: Inform DVLA; check glucose before driving
x: Banned from all driving; surrender the licence
Most insulin users can drive: inform the DVLA and check glucose first.
Tell the GP only; no glucose checks needed
The DVLA must be told, and glucose checked before driving.
Take an extra dose before driving
That would cause hypos; check glucose (≥5 mmol/L) before driving.

items.name: Levothyroxine
items.how: Synthetic T4, converted to T3 in tissues
hx: Synthetic T3, converted to T4 in tissues
It's T4, converted to the active T3 in tissues.
Stimulates TSH release to boost the thyroid
It replaces T4; TSH falls as a result.
Synthetic TSH, stimulating the thyroid gland
It's synthetic T4 hormone.
se: Over-replacement: palpitations, AF, weight loss, tremor, osteoporosis, angina
items.sewhy: Side effects are those of too much thyroid hormone: palpitations and AF, tremor, weight loss, angina and bone loss, so dose by TSH.

x: Triggers thyroid eye disease
Not the reason; it adds more hormone.
Lowers TSH receptor antibodies
No; it adds more hormone.
Causes hypothyroidism
It adds thyroid hormone, worsening thyrotoxicosis.

ci.why: Speeds cortisol clearance → adrenal crisis; give steroids first
x: Blocks ACTH release → adrenal crisis; give levothyroxine first
Thyroxine speeds cortisol breakdown; replace steroids first.
Raises aldosterone → hypertension; give spironolactone first
Not aldosterone; cortisol clearance rises.
Speeds cortisol clearance → Cushing's; cut the steroid dose
Faster clearance worsens the deficiency (crisis); give steroids first.

ci.why: Raised O₂ demand → angina or MI; start low (25 μg)
x: Coronary vasospasm → MI; avoid completely
It raises O₂ demand; start low rather than avoiding it.
Raised O₂ demand → angina; start high to get it over quickly
Start low (25 μg) and titrate slowly.
Bradycardia → heart block; start low
It speeds the heart, raising O₂ demand.

items.name: Carbimazole
hx: Block TSH receptors → ↓ T4/T3 release
They inhibit thyroid peroxidase, stopping hormone synthesis.
Destroy thyroid follicular cells → ↓ T4/T3 synthesis
That's radioiodine; carbimazole blocks thyroid peroxidase.
Inhibit thyroid peroxidase → ↑ T4/T3 release
Blocking the enzyme reduces hormone production.
items.sewhy: An idiosyncratic immune reaction can suddenly stop neutrophil production (agranulocytosis), so a sore throat or fever needs an urgent FBC.

x: Thrombocytopenia recurs
The risk is neutropenia (agranulocytosis).
Hepatitis recurs
Not the reason; agranulocytosis recurs.
Neutropenia was mild and self-limiting
It's life-threatening and recurs.

ci.why: Teratogenic (aplasia cutis); use PTU in the first trimester
x: Teratogenic (cleft palate); use carbimazole in the first trimester
Carbimazole is the teratogen (aplasia cutis); PTU is used.
Causes fetal hyperthyroidism; use radioiodine
Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy; PTU is used in the first trimester.
Not teratogenic, but causes miscarriage; stop all treatment
It's teratogenic, and untreated hyperthyroidism is dangerous; use PTU.
PTU can cause kidney failure
The risk is liver failure.
PTU accumulates in bile
Not the reason; PTU is hepatotoxic.
PTU can cause agranulocytosis only
Agranulocytosis is a risk of both, but PTU's specific risk is liver failure.

items.name: Systemic corticosteroids
items.how: Glucocorticoid receptor → broad anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive gene effects
hx: Mineralocorticoid receptor → broad anti-inflammatory gene effects
The anti-inflammatory effects come through the glucocorticoid receptor.
Histamine receptor block → broad anti-allergic effects
They act through the glucocorticoid receptor on many genes.
Glucocorticoid receptor → broad pro-inflammatory and immune-boosting gene effects
They suppress inflammation and immunity.
items.sewhy: Excess glucocorticoid raises glucose, retains salt (hypertension), breaks down bone and muscle (osteoporosis, myopathy), suppresses immunity, impairs mucosal protection and affects mood. It also suppresses the HPA axis, so stopping suddenly causes adrenal crisis.

x: Steroids inactivate antibiotics
No; immunosuppression lets infection spread.
Steroids raise fever dangerously
They mask fever; immunosuppression is the danger.
Steroids cause bacterial resistance
Not resistance; immunosuppression.
Vaccine has no effect at all
Response may be weak, but the danger is the live strain causing disease.
Vaccine triggers an adrenal crisis
No; the live strain can cause disease.
Vaccine causes steroid resistance
No; the live strain can cause disease.

ci.why: Suppressed adrenals can't respond → adrenal crisis; taper
x: Rebound inflammation is the only risk; stop at once
Suppressed adrenals risk a crisis; taper.
Overactive adrenals → Cushing's crisis; stop at once
The adrenals are suppressed, not overactive; taper.
Suppressed thyroid can't respond → myxoedema; taper
It's the adrenals (HPA axis) that are suppressed.
Lowers glucose
Steroids raise glucose.
Raises ketones directly
They raise glucose.
Blocks insulin absorption
No; they raise glucose (insulin resistance, gluconeogenesis).
↑ gastric emptying and diarrhoea
The concern is ulcers and bleeding.
↓ PPI absorption
No interaction; ulcer and bleeding risk rises.
↑ H. pylori resistance
No; ulcer and bleeding risk.
Lithium toxicity
No interaction; steroids can cause psychosis.
Benzodiazepine withdrawal
Not related; steroids can cause psychosis.
Dementia
Not dementia; steroid psychosis (and mood change).

items.name: Bisphosphonates
items.how: Bind bone mineral and inhibit osteoclasts
hx: Bind bone mineral and stimulate osteoblasts
They inhibit osteoclasts (less resorption); they don't build bone directly.
Mimic PTH to build new bone
That's teriparatide; bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclasts.
Block RANKL to stop osteoclasts forming
That's denosumab; bisphosphonates bind bone and poison osteoclasts.
items.sewhy: Tablets irritate the oesophagus if they lodge (take upright with water). Strongly suppressing bone turnover impairs repair (jaw osteonecrosis, atypical fractures), and lowering resorption can drop calcium.

x: Tablet lodges → oesophageal varices
Varices come from portal hypertension; the tablet causes ulceration.
Absorption fails, so no effect
The danger is the tablet ulcerating the oesophagus.
The tablet triggers achalasia
No; it lodges and ulcerates.

ci.why: Reflux of the tablet damages the oesophagus
x: Lying down blocks absorption completely
The reason is oesophageal damage from reflux.
Lying down causes postural hypotension
Not BP; reflux damages the oesophagus.
Lying down raises jaw osteonecrosis risk
No; reflux of the tablet damages the oesophagus.

ci.why: Lowers calcium further; correct first (and vitamin D)
x: Raises calcium too fast; correct first
They lower calcium; correct it (and vitamin D) first.
Lowers phosphate dangerously; give phosphate
The concern is calcium falling.
Lowers calcium further; give vitamin D afterwards
Correct calcium and vitamin D before starting.
Hepatically excreted; hepatotoxic IV
They're renally excreted, and IV doses are nephrotoxic.
Renally excreted; causes hyperkalaemia
The concern is accumulation and IV nephrotoxicity.
Accumulates in bone, causing fractures
Not the reason; renal excretion and nephrotoxicity.

items.name: Calcium + vitamin D
hx: Replaces calcium and calcitriol (active vitamin D)
Adcal-D3 contains colecalciferol (inactive vitamin D3), not calcitriol.
Replaces calcium and phosphate
It replaces calcium and vitamin D3.
Blocks PTH to retain calcium
It simply replaces calcium and vitamin D.
items.sewhy: Calcium salts commonly cause constipation and GI upset.

x: Lowers calcium too fast
It raises calcium further.
Raises phosphate further
The concern is calcium.
Causes vitamin D deficiency
No; it raises calcium further.
More oxalate in the urine
The issue is extra urinary calcium.
Less urine output
No; more calcium in the urine.
More urate in the urine
No; more calcium.

ci.why: Granulomas make extra active vitamin D → hypercalcaemia
x: Granulomas absorb calcium → hypocalcaemia
Granulomas activate vitamin D, raising calcium.
Granulomas make PTH → hypercalcaemia
They make active vitamin D (1α-hydroxylase), not PTH.
Steroids for sarcoid block calcium absorption
Not the reason; granulomas make active vitamin D.
